title: Faelan's Secret Return
markdown:
The winds sighed over the sharp shoulders of the Whispering Peaks, a land of volcanic breath where meadows shimmered with ash and warm springs bubbled beneath rocks as black as a raven’s deepest shadow. Here, where the air itself tasted of fire and stone, lived an elf named Faelan.

Faelan was mountain-bred, eyes as keen as a hawk’s, boots always dusted with the fine grey powder of his home. He moved with a quiet grace, like the shadow of a cloud drifting over a sun-baked slope. His constant companion, darting and chattering at his heels, was a pine marten named Ink. Ink, with fur the colour of burnt honey and eyes like polished obsidian, was more than a pet. He was Faelan’s shadow, his confidant, and often his silent advisor. Ink’s ability to sniff out hidden paths, and his uncanny knack for knowing when Faelan was fretting, had saved them from many a pickle. A little twitch of the nose was a language Faelan always heeded.

This particular morning, Faelan’s brow was furrowed tighter than a knot in an ancient pine. He clutched a small intricately carved wooden bird in his hand. “Ink,” he whispered, voice a mere breath against the vastness of the mountainside, “we must return this to Lady Evangeline’s grand house before the sun is high. She lent it to me, a gesture of great favour, and it seems I’ve kept it a touch too long. The last thing I need is a fuss from her or her fluttering attendants.” He wanted to slip it back onto her windowsill, unnoticed, a secret returned to its secret keeper. Some elves had a peculiar talent for borrowing things, and an even more peculiar aversion to admitting it. This was not dishonesty so much as a diplomatic discomfort with perceived tardiness.

Faelan and Ink set off, boots crunching on the volcanic scree, a sound like the cracking of tiny ice shards. The landscape unfurled before them: stark, magnificent, alive with the earth’s deep hum. Ash meadows stretched like grey velvet, punctuated by the occasional puff of steam from a hidden vent. Ink, ever vigilant, would freeze mid-stride, sharp ears twitching at the distant cry of a mountain hawk. Faelan, though outwardly calm, felt a familiar prickle of anxiety, a fluttering in his chest like a trapped moth. His mountain upbringing had taught him to observe, to understand the subtle shifts in wind and weather. It had not quite taught him how to navigate the labyrinthine social currents of the valley nobles, with their whispered judgements and scrutinising eyes.

Now, as they rounded a jagged outcrop, a sight unfolded that made Faelan pause, hand instinctively tightening on the wooden bird. A vast flock of shaggy mountain goats milled about, bells tinkling like distant wind chimes. And amongst them, a colossal figure with skin like rough-hewn stone and a beard tangled with stray bits of wool: an ogre. Faelan tensed, ready to dart back into the cover of the rocks, heart giving a startled thump. But Ink gave a soft chirp, a sound that meant wait and see.

The ogre, far from the snarling brutes of legend, was meticulously grooming a small woolly kid goat with a large, surprisingly gentle hand. He noticed Faelan and Ink, massive head tilting slightly.

“Well met, little travellers,” boomed his voice, deep and resonant like the rumble of distant thunder, yet surprisingly devoid of menace. “Lost your way, have you? Or perhaps admiring the splendid flock? They are rather magnificent, aren’t they? Took me all morning to get this one’s coat just so. A bit of mud, you see, from that particularly squishy patch by the waterfall.” He offered a smile, revealing a surprisingly even set of surprisingly clean teeth. “Would you care for some water? Fresh from the glacier melt. Pure and invigorating. Or perhaps a bit of cloudberry tart? Baked it myself this morning. A touch of soot in the crust, perhaps, but the berries are exceptionally sweet. Picked them myself, at dawn.”

Faelan, utterly bewildered, found himself nodding, anxiety momentarily eclipsed by sheer surprise. He had expected to be chased. Instead he was being offered refreshments by an ogre shepherd whose manners were more polished than any duke he had ever encountered. Ink, meanwhile, was investigating a particularly interesting tuft of wool on the ogre’s worn leather boot, clearly unconcerned. The ogre, whose name was Borin, spoke of the best grazing spots, the peculiar habits of his flock (apparently they had a penchant for singing off-key), and the subtle differences in the flavour of mountain herbs, all with an air of quiet refinement. Faelan found himself relaxing, the tension of his secret mission momentarily forgotten in the face of such unexpected courtesy.

Borin, learning of Faelan’s general direction, pointed a thick calloused finger towards a less-travelled pass. “That way,” he rumbled, voice a comforting vibration, “will take you closer to the eastern slopes. It’s a bit of a shortcut, if you don’t mind a touch of a climb. But mind the Glimmering Crags. There’s a dragon that rests there, you see. Sleeps like a giant, coiled and warm near the black rock, a beautiful thing to behold. Best to give her a wide berth. She’s no trouble if left undisturbed, but she doesn’t take kindly to being startled. A sudden noise, and she might just puff out a little smoke, and that can be quite inconvenient.” He winked, a slow deliberate movement of his heavy eyelids.

Faelan thanked Borin profusely, mind still reeling. He and Ink hurried on, the ogre’s kindness a warm ember in Faelan’s chest. Soon the landscape shifted. Jagged obsidian-like rocks jutted from the earth, surfaces polished by wind and time to a glassy sheen. And there, nestled amongst them, was the dragon. A magnificent creature, scales the colour of molten gold, each one catching the sunlight. Its vast body was curled like a living furnace, exhaling slow plumes of steam that rose and dissipated into the thin mountain air. Faelan felt a shiver, not of fear, but of profound awe, as he and Ink crept past, footsteps as soft as falling snow. The dragon barely stirred, a colossal slumbering titan. So close to home, and all this time he had been more frightened of a lady’s attendants.

The path Borin had suggested led them eventually to the outskirts of the valley where Lady Evangeline resided. Her house, perched precariously on a cliff edge, was a confection of spires and balconies, a whimsical structure that seemed to defy gravity. With Ink darting ahead, a furry scout navigating the shadows with practised ease, Faelan managed to creep to a low-lying windowsill, obscured by thick climbing ivy. He placed the wooden bird gently inside, a silent apology for his tardiness and a whispered thank you for her kindness. As he straightened, ready to make his quiet retreat, he heard a faint rustle. It was Ink, nudging something with his nose. Faelan looked closer. A small discarded embroidery needle, its silver glint catching the fading light. He recognised it instantly. It was Lady Evangeline’s, the one she had been searching for, the one she had vaguely mentioned might have been misplaced. He had borrowed that too, weeks ago, to mend a tear in his own satchel, intending to return it promptly. A sheepish grin spread across Faelan’s face. The wooden bird was returned, and in a strange unexpected twist, he had also unknowingly returned a needle he had borrowed. His secret was safe, and so was another.

Returning to their small cottage nestled in a sheltered hollow, a place that smelled perpetually of dried herbs and woodsmoke, Faelan felt a lightness he had not expected. The anxiety that had clung to him like a damp cloak had lifted. He and Ink shared a simple meal of roasted root vegetables and plump sweet berries. Later, as twilight painted the sky in hues of lavender and rose, a few of Faelan’s closest friends gathered. They brought warm hearth-bread, crust baked to a perfect golden brown, and stories of their own days. The crackle of the small fire, the gentle murmur of conversation, and the shared warmth of their company felt like a cosy embrace.

Faelan, watching Ink chase a stray ember across the hearth, felt a quiet confidence bloom. He had faced the fuss he feared, found courtesy in an ogre’s tart, and put two borrowed things back where they belonged. Lady Evangeline might never mention the needle. Sometimes the best secrets stayed gracefully unacknowledged, which suited an elf who still preferred windowsills to drawing rooms.
characters: Faelan (a hawk-eyed mountain elf), Ink (a burnt-honey pine marten)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
